text:
Government
U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman voted yes on H.R. 4219, a bill to authorize invasive species teams
U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman voted yes on H.R. 4219, which would give statutory authority to the National Wildlife Refuge System’s Invasive Species Strike Team program; the measure passed 371-33.
U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman, a Republican who represents Arkansas' 4th Congressional District, voted yes on H.R. 4219, a bill that would authorize the Invasive Species Strike Team program, in the U.S. House on Sept. 14, 2026, according to the U.S. Congress.
The question was On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended. The measure passed. The tally was 371-33.
The bill's title is: "National Wildlife Refuge System Invasive Species Strike Team Act of 2025."
A Congressional Research Service summary of the bill, as reported to the House, states the following: This bill provides statutory authority for the Invasive Species Strike Team program carried out by the National Wildlife Refuge System within the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS). This program operates teams in each FWS region that coordinate with public and private entities to address invasive species and related conservation issues in and around the National Wildlife Refuge System. The bill requires FWS to report to Congress on the program's work and progress towards addressing invasive species that pose a major concern to the environment, human health, or the economy.
U.S. Rep. Ed Case sponsored the bill.
Congressional bills can originate in either the U.S. House of Representatives or the U.S. Senate, except for revenue-related measures, which must begin in the House. After introduction, bills are assigned to committees for review, hearings, amendments and debate before they can advance to a vote in each chamber. If both chambers approve identical versions, the legislation is sent to the president, who may sign it into law or veto it. Congress operates in two-year terms, with each term numbered sequentially and divided into two annual sessions. The legislative process and official bill records are maintained by the U.S. Congress and published through Congress.gov.
House roll-call records list each representative's position and report separate totals for yeas, nays, "present" and "not voting," according to the Office of the Clerk. A "not voting" entry does not explain why no vote was recorded and is distinct from answering "present." The House can also pass measures by voice vote, without a record of each member’s position. A bill passed by the House must also pass the Senate in identical form before it can be sent to the president.
